name: Mexico
summary_text: Mexico pairs meaningful legal progress with one of the world's highest tolls of violence against transgender people. Twenty-two of its 32 states offer administrative legal gender recognition, Mexico City and Nayarit have criminalised transfemicide, marriage equality is nationwide, and constitutional anti-discrimination protections exist. Against that, 71 trans or gender-diverse people were murdered in a single recent year — the second-highest figure in the Americas after Brazil — with organised crime increasingly involved and impunity near-total. The victims are overwhelmingly local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit, not tourists; violence is also highly concentrated by region. In major tourist destinations and central Mexico City, heavily policed and progressively governed, a trans visitor's everyday risk is closer to harassment than violence. The dominant hazard for any traveller is Mexico's general crime environment. Use the Admin Divisions view: state-level scores range from among Latin America's best (Mexico City) to levels comparable with its most dangerous regions.

sources.title: Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim_summary: Human Rights Watch (Mar 2025): 'Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges' — advances in legal gender recognition and hate-crime response alongside persistent violence and implementation gaps.

sources.title: “I Just Want to Contribute to Society”: The Need for Legal Gender Recognition in Tabasco, Mexico | HRW
sources.claim_summary: HRW report 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society' (March 2024) on the need for legal gender recognition in Tabasco, Mexico: murders and violence against trans people (e.g. Karina Gómez found in the Carrizal River with a concrete block tied to her feet, Aug 2023) rest on daily discrimination amplified by obstacles to legal name/gender recognition - the mismatch between lived and legal identities leaves trans people exposed.

sources.title: Transfemicide becomes a crime in a ‘watershed’ moment for Mexico City | Transgender | The Guardian
sources.claim_summary: The Guardian (July 2024): transfemicide becomes a crime in Mexico City - the 'Paola Buenrostro law' approved 18 July 2024, a 'watershed' moment named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished.

AP (Jan 2024): 'Wave of transgender killings in Mexico spurs protests' — at least three transgender people killed in early 2024, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca shot in Mexico City, drawing LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests.

sources.title: Federal and Local Authorities in Mexico Must Step Up Efforts to Prevent and Punish Acts of Violence Against Trans People
sources.claim_summary: IACHR press release (2024): the Inter-American Commission expressed concern over violence against trans and gender-diverse people in Mexico and urged protective measures.

Agencia Presentes (Jun 2024): 'Violence against trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders increased in the last year' in Mexico — data report on rising attacks against trans people and killings of defenders.

sources.title: LGBTQ+ people in Mexico face significant threats of violence, even as formal rights are extended | LSE United States Politics and Policy
sources.claim_summary: LSE USAPP commentary by Caroline Beer (Nov 2024): LGBTQ+ people in Mexico face significant threats of violence even as formal rights are extended - analysis of the gap between legal rights and lived safety.
Government of Canada travel advice for Mexico (updated Aug 2026): 'Exercise a high degree of caution' with regional advisories. General travel advice, not trans-specific.

sources.title: LGBTQIA+ travel in Mexico | Intrepid Travel US
sources.claim_summary: Intrepid Travel country guide ('LGBTQIA+ travel in Mexico'): Mexico City has a large queer scene, annual Pride and LGBT-friendly hotels, bars and tours, plus Cancun as a hotspot; the guide also notes Mexico's indigenous 'third gender' muxes of Oaxaca and advises caution outside tourist hubs.

sources.title: Ciudad de México tipifica el delito de transfeminicidio: estos son los cambios a la ley | CNN
sources.claim_summary: CNN en Español (July 2024): Mexico City's Congress approved the 'Paola Buenrostro' law criminalising transfemicide - the second federal entity to do so after Nayarit (March); named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished.

sources.title: Mexican state approves gay civil unions | Mail & Guardian
sources.claim_summary: Mail & Guardian (Jan 2007): the northern Mexican state of Coahuila became the third Latin-American jurisdiction to approve gay civil unions (20-13 vote), following Mexico City and Buenos Aires - but the law bars same-sex couples from adopting or getting custody; PRI deputy Julieta Lopez called it 'a sensible response' to discrimination; PAN called it 'an attack against the family'.
